body.text: In May 2020, Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, a senior leader of the Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (NC), was still under house detention when he picked a fight with his own party.

Kashmir was only beginning to emerge from the political paralysis that followed the Narendra Modi government’s unilateral decision on August 5, 2019, to abrogate Article 370, which had governed the constitutional relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the rest of India. After months of detention and a near-total political freeze imposed by the Union government in the days leading up to that decision, the region’s political leadership was slowly returning to public life.

On May 24, 2020, NC leader Tanvir Sadiq wrote an opinion piece in a regional newspaper calling on New Delhi for “reconciliation”, a “revisit” of the domicile law, and “resumption of political process”. The article prompted Ruhullah, a former cabinet minister and three-time legislator, to challenge his party colleague’s position. “’Revisit’ domicile law? Lift curbs on Internet? ‘LET’ political process be run? Is that all what you are looking for in this reconciliation?” Ruhullah asked in a social media post. “When you ask them to ‘let’ us, it will naturally be on their terms.”

The rebuke made him one of the first political figures to openly criticise New Delhi’s new constitutional order for the region. It also crystallised a dissent that was already taking shape within the party.

Two months later, as tempers flared, NC vice president Omar Abdullah said he would not contest an election as long as Jammu and Kashmir remained a Union Territory, and that the party would challenge the changes “in the highest court in the land”.

A day later, Ruhullah resigned as the National Conference’s chief spokesperson—his first formal break with a party whose political line, he felt, was drifting away from the fight for the region’s special status.
Six years on, the same fault line has brought him to the brink of quitting the party altogether and of giving up the Srinagar Lok Sabha seat he won on an NC ticket in 2024.

Ruhullah’s decision to leave comes midway through the two-year-old Omar Abdullah government, which political observers say has struggled to stand up to New Delhi and its appointed Lieutenant Governor.

Yet observers do not see his resignation as a decisive blow to the NC. While it may add to the pressure of incumbency on Abdullah’s government, they argue it is unlikely to weaken the party at its core. Its larger effect, they say, could be felt in the opposition space—particularly by the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), whose traditional anti-NC constituency Ruhullah is now positioned to contest.

Even a win confined to his own seat, observers told Frontline, could expand the political space available to voices opposed to the post-2019 status quo—beyond a PDP that has been electorally weakened in recent years.
A new contender

Ever since New Delhi stripped Jammu and Kashmir of its special status, Ruhullah has remained an outspoken voice of dissent, representing a widely felt sense of loss in the region. To consolidate anti-abrogation and pro-autonomy sentiment ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the NC fielded him from Srinagar, one of three parliamentary seats in the Kashmir Valley.

His victory gave him a national platform to confront the Modi government over its changes to Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional status. But as his political stature grew, his standing within the party declined. He led a demonstration outside Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s residence over reservation policy, stayed away from campaigning for the NC in the Budgam bypoll, boycotted a Statehood protest in the capital in July, and repeatedly accused the NC leadership of abandoning its commitment to restoring the region’s special status.

His growing political appeal carries implications beyond his troubled relationship with the NC. “In Kashmir, the anti-NC and anti-Delhi space was earlier occupied by separatism, but since separatism was criminalised, that space was represented by the PDP,” said a Srinagar-based political observer who did not wish to be identified. “The core competence of PDP, which is basically to put a plank around anti-NC sentiment, will have a new contender in Ruhullah, who is already tested by the public. The edge will shift from PDP to Ruhullah’s favour.”

Ruhullah, the observer said, is unlikely to contest elections to win a majority. “Even if he wins only his own seat, it would cement a lot many voices who are against the whole politics of status quo. It will encroach on PDP’s space in Kashmir politics but will not impact NC much. Its organisation will remain the same. It has a strong structure, cadre, history and legacy, so it is not easy to displace NC. Many have tried to do so but failed. For now, among the contenders in the race to come up as the primary anti-NC force, Ruhullah seems to lead.”

The observer does not believe Ruhullah would necessarily replace the PDP outright. “But if he leaves the NC, creates a new party, or wins the election again and brings like-minded people, it could create an existential crisis for the PDP. And that is why the PDP does not have much of an answer to what Ruhullah is [currently] doing.”

Meanwhile, Ruhullah’s departure could add to pressure already building on the NC government. Nearly two years since it took office, most of the party’s election promises remain unfulfilled. Abdullah has repeatedly said his government was elected for five years and should be judged only after five. Criticism, even so, has only grown.

Rekha Chowdhary, former professor of political science at Jammu University, said such criticism follows a familiar pattern. “The criticism is natural because once you are in power, then after the honeymoon period is over, the anti-incumbency will start popping up,” she told Frontline. “Generally, the advantage of anti-incumbency goes to the opposition party. But in this case the problem is that PDP is currently too weak to fully capitalise on that opening. That advantage can shift to Ruhullah, but only to the extent that it can help him build a political space for himself. Other than that it is not going to adversely impact the NC.”
A political counterweight?

Ruhullah’s dissent, once confined within the National Conference, has taken on a political identity of its own in the two years since the Assembly election. The Srinagar MP’s confrontational politics has found considerable resonance in Kashmir.

“Ruhullah represents a sentiment and he will continue to represent that sentiment. That sentiment exists within the NC as well,” Chowdhary said. “He is already confident that he has created a political space for himself. That is why he has been taking these positions. He has made it clear that he stands on his own, rather than being dependent on the NC. To that extent, he has already carved out some political space for himself.”

Whether that space is large enough to put the NC in real difficulty remains an open question. Chowdhary noted that Ruhullah, despite the symbolic weight of his departure and a plausible repeat electoral win, remains an individual leader without the organisational strength to fundamentally alter Jammu and Kashmir’s political landscape. “If it is a party versus party, then you can see something changing,” she said. “But party versus an individual is a difficult task. It will certainly have a symbolic effect, in fact, it already has. There might be a possibility of Ruhullah winning again [after resignation]. But I do not see a scenario that changes the politics of Jammu and Kashmir at this point of time and later.”

Even if Ruhullah were to convert that political space into electoral power, Chowdhary questioned what he could ultimately achieve within Kashmir’s existing political arrangement. “If he is replaced and he becomes the Chief Minister, what can be the scenario? He can just raise the issue and that’s all. Raising the issue and having no result,” she said. “So it is only a question of making a statement. He has been making a statement, and even after leaving the party and winning the election, he will be continuing to make that statement.”

Ruhullah has said he will resign on November 3—the 26th death anniversary of his father, Aga Syed Mehdi, a prominent mainstream Shia politician assassinated by militants in 2000. His possible exit would not be the first time the NC has weathered the departure of a prominent elected leader. The party has previously lost three parliamentarians—Shamim Ahmed Shamim, Saifuddin Soz, and Abdul Rashid Kabuli—after ruptures with its leadership.

“Their [Shamim and Soz’s] departure did not fundamentally alter NC’s standing, and Ruhullah’s exit would also be to that extent only,” Chowdhary said. “He does not have as much force as that of a party to change the politics.”
Lack of a mechanism

While Abdullah and Ruhullah have occupied opposing political positions, with Ruhullah’s brand of politics finding greater support on the ground in Kashmir, observers point to a gap between his confrontations with the two governments and any concrete roadmap for the region.

“Ruhullah is not suggesting the way forward or the mechanism for resolution of problems [that concern J&K],” said Gul Mohammed Wani, a retired professor who headed the political science department at Kashmir University. “The mechanism can be democratic, legislative and deliberative for an elected MP, a lawmaker.”

The demands raised by Ruhullah and by the Abdullah government, Wani said, are in many ways similar, as are the mechanisms available to them. “The issues and demands are common to them. Mechanisms are also by and large common to them,” he said. “It still remains a question what Aga Ruhullah expects Omar Abdullah to do and what he is not doing.”
Wani said Ruhullah’s resignation could nonetheless serve as a political signal to the NC government. “It would be a sort of one more wake up call for NC and Omar Abdullah’s government,” he said.

Questions remain, too, about what Ruhullah would achieve by returning to Parliament should he resign and win the seat again. “What is he going to actually do and what is he going to prove out of that remains a mystery,” Wani said. “The elephant in the room is neither Omar nor Ruhullah but the Indian state with Modi and Amit Shah as its managers. So, the main question is what happens to the elephant.”

He added: “It can be a sort of a political experiment that may unfold with Aga Ruhullah’s resignation. But things are not at the structural level. At the fundamental level, things, players, and institutions would be as they are.”

That, Wani said, reflects the narrow political space available to people in Jammu and Kashmir, confined largely to elections. “People are not becoming party to anything,” he said. “It is a type of a situation in which people’s power has remained confined to electoral politics and beyond that, it is nothing.”

New Delhi, he added, has shown little response to demands from either camp. “All these positive signals are not being actually entertained and welcomed by the Indian state,” he said. “Either Delhi is settled down on this thing that we are not going to change anything in Kashmir or maybe they want to build up an opinion in Kashmir that why not to vote for BJP.”
A leverage point?

Ruhullah’s departure may carry consequences beyond the NC and Kashmir’s opposition. Wani believes it could also strengthen Omar Abdullah’s hand with New Delhi. “It may also give some amount of leverage and bargaining power to him [Abdullah] as far as the Centre is concerned,” he said. “Leverage in the sense that if there is no opposition and no demand, what can the Chief Minister do? How is he going to sell his own demands also?”

Abdullah, Wani said, could also point to any erosion in the NC’s electoral space to argue to New Delhi that his government is being constrained from delivering on its promises. The larger question is whether Ruhullah can carry the political gains he made within the NC into an independent political journey—a first in his 24-year career. “Ruhullah’s decision to leave the National Conference is really a test of how much of his political strength belongs to him and how much came from the party,” said another Kashmir-based political observer, who also asked not to be named. “His politics since 2024 has largely been built around opposing the government, but opposition alone cannot create a lasting political base.”

The observer said Ruhullah must now show he can convert personal appeal into an independent organisation with a clear political programme. “Otherwise, leaving the NC could take him from being a strong voice within Kashmir’s politics to a voice with limited electoral reach,” the observer said.
Zaid Bin Shabir is a journalist based in Srinagar.
